look_here_first: GREEN SPRANGLETOP: look for a usually PERENNIAL, often robust bunch with relatively broad bluish-green blades and a terminal head of about 2–15 long slender branches, frequently widely spreading or gently drooping. Branches carry spikelets mostly on ONE side. Then examine ONE mature 4–12 mm spikelet at 10–20×: commonly 4–13 florets (count inside one spikelet), with fairly blunt or NOTCHED, generally awnless or minutely pointed lemmas ~3.5–5 mm long. At the blade–sheath junction verify a SHORT MEMBRANOUS ligule with a fringed margin; in lower sheaths look for optional HIDDEN self-pollinating (cleistogamous) flowers. A flowering-head photo alone cannot prove florets, notches, ligule or hidden heads.

best_field_traits: PERENNIAL: typically stout bunchgrass with a lasting tough base, sometimes locally producing basal tillers; do not infer a root system from a cut stem.

PANICLE BRANCHES: usually about 2–15 slender, long, often widely spreading or nodding branches arranged along a main flowering axis; spikelets on mostly ONE side (secund). Inflorescence branch count is supporting, not uniquely diagnostic.
SPIKELETS: about 4–12 mm long, 4–13 florets PER INDIVIDUAL SPIKELET; count florets on the rachilla, not spikelets on different branches. Fertile florets may spread widely at maturity.
LEMMA: usually ~3.5–5 mm long, 3-veined, often hairy toward lower margins; tip broad, nearly square/obtuse to shallowly notched, awnless or with a tiny mucro, NOT a long threeawn bristle.
LIGULE: actual short membranous inside blade/sheath junction with a fringed/ciliate upper edge; genus treatment typically 0.5–1.5 mm, Flora of North America sometimes 1–2 mm.

SECONDARY HEADS: may produce cleistogamous (closed, self-pollinating) panicles enclosed LOW in leaf sheaths. Seeing one strongly supports ID; failing to find one on a single stalk does not rule species out.
Older names LEPTOCHLOA DUBIA / DIPLACHNE DUBIA are synonyms for the same plant. State-wide nativity or taxonomic flags were NOT newly audited in this visual upgrade.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: FULL HABIT: same individual photographed from tough perennial crown (with any basal tillers) to flowering head; add a centimeter ruler and note if stolons are present.
PANICLE: entire 2–15 branch flowering head with at least one branch showing its mostly one-sided spikelet attachment and where each branch arises along the main axis.
SPIKELET 10–20×: mm ruler beside an intact 4–12 mm spikelet, glumes and rachilla visible so 4–13 FLORETS can be individually counted.
LEMMA 20×: separate a mature 3.5–5 mm lemma and show its approximately flat/square, often shallowly two-notched tip, hair placement and any tiny mucro; do not claim a long awn.
TRUE COLLAR: unfold a blade and measure membranous ligule with finely fringed apex, showing the actual blade/sheath junction (2013 treatment 0.5–1.5 mm; some regional accounts 1–2 mm).
LOW SHEATHS: on the same plant, document an enclosed cleistogamous flowering head when present; absence in one sheath is not a negative ID.
MATCHED COMPARISON: Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata full annual plant plus 2–4 mm 2–4-flowered mature spikelet, both shot at the same scale as Disakisperma.
crew_field_check: Trace a WHOLE rooted individual, not just a detached panicle: green sprangletop normally perennial, annual Dinebra has much finer panicle branches.
Observe the side of a mature flowering branch where spikelets line up. Under magnification, count individual florets inside ONE measured mature spikelet.
Look closely for broad square/obtuse often NOTCHED lemma tip and a genuinely fringed membranous ligule, and optionally a hidden secondary flowering head in a lower sheath.

Compare Dinebra on spikelet LENGTH and floret COUNT as well as habit: Disakisperma 4–12 mm and 4–13 florets, Dinebra commonly ~2–4 mm and 2–4 florets; counts can overlap, so don't decide from four alone.
Two new credited Commons photos show the real species from west Texas but do not demonstrate invisible microscopic anatomy; only mark what is actually visible.

comparisons.key_distinctions: DINEBRA PANICEA subsp. MUCRONATA (mucronate sprangletop): generally a slender ANNUAL with MANY fine ascending branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets with typically 2–4 florets and a much smaller lemma; Green sprangletop is a usually larger PERENNIAL with about 2–15 often widely spreading branches and ~4–12 mm spikelets with 4–13 florets. Both may bear four-flowered spikelets: measure the actual mature spikelet AND inspect rooted habit before deciding. DIPLACHNE FUSCA (bearded sprangletop) can also have long spreading branches; its ligule tends to be much longer and pointed (often ~2–8 mm), and lemma tip shape differs, so confirm with a microscope. Old Leptochloa dubia and Diplachne dubia refer to the same green sprangletop taxon, not new cards. Do not mistake a single branch of the panicle for a whole spikelet.

field_matrix.this_species: Usually perennial, ~2–15 sometimes spreading branches; spikelets ~4–12 mm with 4–13 florets
field_matrix.look_alike: Usually slender annual, many much finer branches; spikelets ~2–4 mm with ~2–4 florets
field_matrix.quick_rule: Four florets overlaps; branch shape alone does not decide. Compare mature spikelet size AND roots.

field_matrix.this_species: Short ~0.5–1.5 mm ciliate-fringed membrane, blunt/commonly notched lemma, occasionally hidden low-sheath panicles
field_matrix.look_alike: Often longer more pointed 2–8 mm membranous ligule and more acute lemma tip, hidden low-sheath inflorescence absent in regional key
field_matrix.quick_rule: Don't use branch spread alone; the ligule and mature lemma provide the better distinction.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: GREEN SPRANGLETOP (Disakisperma dubium, formerly Leptochloa dubia): look for a native warm-season bunchgrass with wide open, often drooping flowering head and one-sided rows of multiflowered spikelets. Check a tough perennial tuft and short fringed membranous ligule; the latter must be viewed from INSIDE the blade/sheath junction. Locally archived regional images show habitat clumps, external collar junctions, full panicles and floral parts, but still lack a proven connected exposed root crown and scaled free inner ligule. Published flora describes no stolons or rhizomes; do not interpret a soil-contact tuft as demonstrated root anatomy.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalikes: DINEBRA PANICEA subsp. MUCRONATA (mucronate sprangletop): generally a slender ANNUAL with MANY fine ascending branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets with typically 2–4 florets and a much smaller lemma; Green sprangletop is a usually larger PERENNIAL with about 2–15 often widely spreading branches and ~4–12 mm spikelets with 4–13 florets. Both may bear four-flowered spikelets: measure the actual mature spikelet AND inspect rooted habit before deciding. DIPLACHNE FUSCA (bearded sprangletop) can also have long spreading branches; its ligule tends to be much longer and pointed (often ~2–8 mm), and lemma tip shape differs, so confirm with a microscope. Old Leptochloa dubia and Diplachne dubia refer to the same green sprangletop taxon, not new cards. Do not mistake a single branch of the panicle for a whole spikelet.
photo_targets: ACTUAL ROOTED BASE: gently lift an authenticated green sprangletop individual, rinse enough soil to show attached fibrous roots, compact crown and basal tillers, then photograph WHOLE same plant with flower culm and 1-cm scale; also photograph plant upright before lifting (with collection permission). Do not borrow another species' roots.

TRUE INNER LIGULE: fold blade forward to expose short inner membranous fringe at blade/sheath junction and image from adaxial side using a 1-mm ruler and sharp macro; distinguish separate collar hairs.

FLOWERING ARCHITECTURE: one entirely attached mature panicle, each long branch and the orientation of overlapping multiflowered spikelets, beside a centimeter scale (mostly already covered by existing photos).
MEASURED REPRODUCTIVE DETAIL: intact single spikelet with 1-mm scale and countable florets, plus photographed basal glumes and an isolated blunt/notched 3-veined lemma with the same scale.
LOW SHEATH: authentic enclosing basal cleistogamous spikelet if naturally present; do not manufacture this feature or require it for every field observation.
MATCHED DIFFERENTIAL: compare Dinebra and Diplachne same-scale root/ligule/lemma photos with individually cleared licenses, preserving their distinct original IDs.

measured_diagnostic_key.habit: Mostly perennial tufted or occasionally stoloniferous; document rooted crown rather than assuming perennial from a clipped flowering stem.
measured_diagnostic_key.terminal_panicle_cm: 10–45 long, 3–25 wide; raceme-like unilateral branches commonly 5–15
measured_diagnostic_key.spikelets_mm: 4–12, 4–13 florets, usually nearly sessile on unilateral branches
measured_diagnostic_key.lemma_mm: 3.5–5.0, usually 3-veined, often hairy on margins/below, apex sometimes shallowly bifid, awnless or minutely mucronate
measured_diagnostic_key.cleistogamy: Additional closed-flowering spikelets may be hidden in LOWER leaf sheaths; photograph on the same plant without claiming absence when not found.

look_alike_field_key.compare: Generally annual with 2–4(–5) florets per much smaller 2–4 mm spikelet and lemma about 0.9–1.7 mm in regional descriptions. Check rooted annual base, glumes, and true floret count; don't infer species from thin one-sided branches alone.
Require mature lemma length, floret count, ligule, and hidden lower-sheath inflorescences; retain Disakisperma sp. if structures are missing.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial bunch; ~2–15 long, often spreading one-sided branches
field_id_short_tiles.details: Read the same-species habit and flowering photos in panels 3–6, 10 and 15 (indices 2,3,4,5,9,14). The regional bunch grass bears an open panicle with commonly 2–15 spreading or drooping branches and multiple spikelets along each flowering branch. Panel 3 (index 2) shows a real basal leaf tuft among rock, but roots and their attachment are NOT exposed; DO NOT call this a proved rooted crown. A branch is not a spikelet.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FLOWERING ARCHITECTURE PHOTOGRAPHED — ATTACHED EXPOSED ROOTS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Short ~0.5–1.5 mm membranous ligule with fringed edge
field_id_short_tiles.details: See photos 1–2 and 7 (indices 0,1,6). Direct inspection of original pixels shows a green exterior blade–sheath junction and pale collar tissue in photo 1, and Jim Conrad's small junction/lip from Uvalde in photo 7. The true free inner membranous ligule edge, its tiny marginal fringe, and a 1-mm scale are NOT convincingly isolated in these pixels. Fold back the blade and photograph from INSIDE the sheath (adaxial view); never substitute collar hairs or an outside white collar lip.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL JUNCTION PHOTOS PRESENT — INNER FRINGED LIGULE WITH SCALE STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS INSIDE ONE SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.details: Use Jim Conrad's attached and separated spikelets (panels 8–9, indices 7–8) and Bob Harms' photographed floral-unit series (panels 11–14, indices 10–13) to teach a spikelet versus its internal florets. The published 4–12 mm and 4–13 floret ranges are not measured in these original pixels; capture an intact mature spikelet beside a 1-mm ruler and count the florets within that same spikelet before labeling anatomical counts.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · EXPOSE THE TWO BASAL GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower ~2.3–4.8 mm; upper ~3.3–6 mm in published key
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panel 8 shows loose floral units, and the Harms scientific series in panels 11–12 shows detached material (indices 7,10,11), but no verified same-voucher sequence unambiguously labels both basal glumes at millimeter resolution. Published lower and upper glume lengths are references, NOT measurements from these photos. Dissect and show both glumes remaining at the base of a single measured mature spikelet before adding arrows.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · EXAMINE THE BLUNT LEMMA AND LOW SHEATHS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lemma ~3.5–5 mm, 3-veined, blunt/notched; no long awn
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panel 8 (index 7) shows teased-apart actual Uvalde floral material with blunt-looking tips; panels 11–12 (indices 10–11) supply more Central Texas comparative details. Source references describe a broad, often notched lemma tip; a calibrated individual floret/lemma photo and verified 3-vein count remain missing. Lower, sheath-enclosed cleistogamous spikelets are described in botanical literature but not demonstrated by these images; absence from one sheath proves nothing.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MEASURED LEMMA TIP AND OPTIONAL SHEATH HEAD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP
field_id_short_tiles.short: Larger usually perennial spikelets vs Dinebra's small annual units
field_id_short_tiles.details: Final panel 16 (index 15) is explicitly Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata, a DIFFERENT species, shown under its own source determination and individual CC BY-NC terms; don't count it as D. dubium evidence. Compare with same-species head photos 6, 10 and 15 (indices 5,9,14). Green sprangletop is a perennial bunchgrass with larger multiflowered spikelets, while Dinebra species often have smaller annual heads. There is overlap in floret count; confirm true lower growth habit, glumes, lemma and ligule, especially against Diplachne fusca.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY DIFFERENTIAL; SAME-SCALE LOCAL ANATOMY MISSING

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Green sprangletop — crown, inner ligule and blunt lemma are the finish gate
steps: Panels 3 and 10 (indices 2,9): recognize a tuft and whole flowering form, but do not call soil contact actual root anatomy.
Panels 1–2 and 7 (indices 0,1,6): distinguish externally visible collar tissue from the FREE inner ligule; source photos are real but still lack ruler/inner opened view.
Panels 9 and 11–12 (indices 8,10,11): compare multiflowered spikelets and separated floral units, never assigning microscope-scale glume/lemma identities beyond resolution.
Panel 16 (index 15) is another species (Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata), useful as contrast but not direct evidence for D. dubium.

Collect one proven green sprangletop specimen with permission and photograph connected fibrous roots, tight base/crown, true inner membrane with 1-mm bar, whole flowering head and isolated square/notched lemma. Published sources describe no stolons or rhizomes; do not invent these structures.

AZ Grasses has a photograph specifically labeled green sprangletop roots and University of Arizona a labeled ligule photo. Their image-level website republication rights remain unproven: reference links only.
